stem: During digestion, enzymes completely break apart an unbranched chain of 10 glucose monomers, releasing 10 free glucose molecules. Which statement correctly describes this reaction and the water involved?

choices.choice_text: It is dehydration synthesis, and 9 water molecules are released.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you link 'water released' to any reaction involving monomers, but dehydration synthesis builds polymers, and this chain is being broken apart. Fix: breaking a polymer into monomers is hydrolysis.

choices.choice_text: It is hydrolysis, and 9 water molecules are released.
choices.rationale: Tempting because you named the right reaction, but you reversed the direction of water. Hydrolysis means 'splitting with water': each bond breaks as a water molecule is added. Fix: hydrolysis uses water; dehydration synthesis releases it.

choices.choice_text: It is hydrolysis, and 9 water molecules are consumed.
choices.rationale: Breaking a polymer into monomers is hydrolysis, which uses one water molecule per bond broken, adding an H to one monomer and an OH to the other. An unbranched chain of 10 monomers has 9 bonds between them, so 9 water molecules are consumed.

choices.choice_text: It is hydrolysis, and 10 water molecules are consumed.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you count monomers instead of bonds. Water is used once per bond, and a chain of 10 monomers has only 9 links between them. Fix: for an unbranched chain, bonds = monomers minus 1.

verification: EK 1.3.A.1: hydrolysis cleaves a polymer bond by adding water (H to one monomer, OH to the other); explainer: one water consumed per bond broken. Unbranched chain of n=10 monomers has n-1=9 bonds -> 9 H2O consumed.
author_flags: Context is a carbohydrate chain but no carbohydrate structure detail is required (1.4 exclusion respected). Seed (sugar isomers/transport) used only as a difficulty anchor; different idea.

stem: An enzyme made of a single polypeptide chain is treated with a chemical that breaks hydrogen bonds but does not break covalent bonds. After treatment, the enzyme can no longer bind its substrate. Which statement best explains the loss of function?

choices.choice_text: Broken hydrogen bonds unfold the helices, sheets and 3D shape, changing the active site, while the amino acid sequence stays the same.
choices.rationale: Secondary structure depends on hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms, and tertiary shape depends partly on hydrogen bonds between R groups. Breaking them changes the folded shape, including the active site, so the substrate no longer fits. The peptide bonds are covalent, so the primary structure stays intact.

choices.choice_text: The peptide bonds linking the amino acids are broken, so the enzyme falls apart into free amino acids that cannot bind the substrate.
choices.rationale: Tempting because the enzyme clearly 'came apart' in function. But peptide bonds are covalent, and this chemical breaks only hydrogen bonds. Fix: check which bond type a treatment breaks before deciding which structural level is lost.

choices.choice_text: The separate polypeptide chains of the enzyme drift apart, so the quaternary structure needed to form the active site is lost.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you assume every enzyme has quaternary structure. Quaternary structure exists only when a protein has more than one polypeptide, and this enzyme has one chain. Fix: name quaternary structure only for multi-chain proteins.

choices.choice_text: The chemical changes the order of amino acids in the chain, giving the enzyme a new primary structure that no longer fits the substrate.
choices.rationale: Tempting because sequence does determine shape. But the amino acid order is set by covalent peptide bonds, which this chemical leaves intact; only a mutation would change the sequence. Fix: the sequence stays the same here; the folding is what changes.

verification: EK 1.7.A.4 (secondary structure from backbone H-bonds), EK 1.7.A.5 (tertiary from H-bonds, hydrophobic, ionic, disulfide), EK 1.7.A.6 (quaternary only with multiple polypeptides; all levels determine function), EK 1.7.A.1 (peptide bonds covalent). Single chain + only H-bonds broken -> secondary/tertiary disrupted, primary intact, no quaternary.
author_flags: Touches denaturation language lightly (3.2 overlap) but answer rests on 1.7 structure levels. Seed (surface hydrophobic aggregation) not reused.

stem: A student writes: "Bacteria have no membrane-bound organelles, so the inside of a bacterial cell has no internal organization at all." Which statement best corrects the student's claim?

choices.choice_text: Bacteria have a true nucleus surrounded by a double membrane, which keeps their DNA separate from the rest of the cytoplasm.
choices.rationale: Tempting because bacterial DNA does sit in one area of the cell. But that area is not enclosed by a membrane, so it is not a nucleus. Fix: a membrane-bound nucleus is a eukaryotic feature.

choices.choice_text: Bacteria contain small mitochondria, which form a separate compartment where cellular respiration happens.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you mix up the direction of endosymbiosis. Mitochondria descended from free-living prokaryotes that were engulfed by a host cell; bacteria do not contain mitochondria. Fix: mitochondria came from bacteria, not inside bacteria.

choices.choice_text: Bacteria have an endoplasmic reticulum and a Golgi apparatus that divide the cytoplasm into compartments.
choices.rationale: Tempting because these membranes are what organize a eukaryotic cell. But the endomembrane system is a eukaryotic feature that bacteria lack. Fix: eukaryotes partition the cell with internal membranes; prokaryotes do not.

choices.choice_text: Bacteria lack membrane-bound organelles but have specialized internal regions, such as an area where DNA is concentrated.
choices.rationale: This keeps the true part of the claim and fixes the false part. Prokaryotes typically lack membrane-bound organelles, but they do have specialized internal regions, while eukaryotes use internal membranes to partition the cell into compartments.

verification: EK 2.10.A.2 (prokaryotes typically lack membrane-bound organelles but have specialized internal regions); EK 2.10.A.3 (eukaryotic internal membranes partition); EK 2.10.A.1 (mitochondria evolved from free-living prokaryotes). Brief common_point_loss names 'claiming prokaryotes have no internal organization at all'.
author_flags: Correct choice gives the DNA region (nucleoid) as the example of a specialized region; the explainer does not name a specific region. Checker: confirm this example is acceptable at CED scope. Seed tested double-membrane engulfment evidence; this item tests the prokaryote/eukaryote compartmentalization contrast instead.

stem: When phospholipids are mixed into water, they spontaneously form hollow spheres whose wall is a bilayer, with water both inside and outside the sphere. Which statement best explains how the phospholipids are arranged in this wall?

choices.choice_text: The fatty-acid tails face the water on both surfaces, because the tails form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you swap which part of the phospholipid is water-loving. The fatty-acid tails are nonpolar hydrocarbon chains and cannot hydrogen bond with water. Fix: the tails are hydrophobic and point away from water.

choices.choice_text: The phosphate heads face the water on both surfaces, and the fatty-acid tails face each other in the interior, away from water.
choices.rationale: Phospholipids are amphipathic: the hydrophilic phosphate head interacts with water and the hydrophobic tails avoid it. With water on both sides, two layers form with heads facing each water surface and tails tucked together in the middle, the same arrangement as the plasma membrane.

choices.choice_text: The phosphate heads face inward toward each other in the middle, and the tails face outward toward the water.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you picture the heads clustering together. But that would put the hydrophobic tails in contact with water on both sides, the least stable arrangement. Fix: heads go wherever water is; tails go where water is not.

choices.choice_text: The phospholipids are joined to each other by covalent bonds, which lock them into a rigid sheet that keeps water out.
choices.rationale: Tempting because a membrane seems like a solid wall. But the bilayer is held together by hydrophobic interactions, not covalent bonds, and its lipids and proteins drift within it, as the fluid mosaic model describes. Fix: the membrane is fluid, not a rigid covalent sheet.

verification: EK 2.3.A.1 (hydrophilic heads face out, hydrophobic tails face in); explainer: amphipathic phospholipids, heads face watery cytoplasm/extracellular fluid, tails inward; EK 2.3.B.1 fluid mosaic (mobile components).
author_flags: Seed tested multipass membrane-protein orientation; this item tests phospholipid orientation instead, so the seed answer is not taught here.

stem: An enzyme speeds up the breakdown of its substrate into two products. Compared with the same reaction without the enzyme, which statement about the catalyzed reaction is correct?

choices.choice_text: The enzyme adds energy to the substrate, giving it enough energy to break apart into products.
choices.rationale: Tempting because a faster reaction feels like it needs extra energy. But enzymes do not supply energy; they lower the energy barrier the substrate must get over. Fix: say enzymes lower activation energy, never that they add energy.

choices.choice_text: The enzyme makes the reaction release more energy overall, which is why the products form faster.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you link speed to the amount of energy released. An enzyme does not change the energy of the reactants or products, so the overall energy change is the same. Fix: enzymes change the rate, not the overall energy difference.

choices.choice_text: The enzyme lowers the activation energy by binding to any molecule that is about the same size as its substrate.
choices.rationale: Tempting because the activation-energy part is right. But binding depends on the substrate's shape and charge fitting the active site, not just its size, which is why enzymes are specific. Fix: specificity comes from shape and charge fit.

choices.choice_text: The enzyme lowers the activation energy, but the overall energy change from reactants to products stays the same.
choices.rationale: Enzymes are catalysts: by binding the substrate in the active site, they lower the activation energy so the reaction proceeds faster. They do not change the starting or ending energy of the reaction, so the overall energy difference stays the same.

verification: EK 3.1.A.1 (enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy); EK 3.1.A.2 (substrate shape/charge must fit active site); brief common_point_loss: 'saying enzymes add energy'. Catalysts do not alter reactant/product energies (overall energy change unchanged).
author_flags: No seed. Choice B's 'overall energy change' is described conceptually; no Gibbs equation used (3.3 exclusion respected).

stem: Joining molecule X to molecule Y to form XY requires an input of energy and does not happen on its own in the cell. The cell makes XY in two steps: an enzyme first transfers a phosphate group from ATP to X, and the phosphorylated X then reacts with Y. Which statement best explains how this lets the cell make XY?

choices.choice_text: Energy released by ATP hydrolysis is coupled, through the phosphate transfer, to the energy-requiring formation of XY.
choices.rationale: This is energy coupling. Removing a phosphate from ATP releases energy, and moving that phosphate onto X makes X more reactive. The energy released by ATP hydrolysis is greater than the energy XY formation requires, so the combined process can proceed.

choices.choice_text: ATP breaks down and releases heat, and that heat warms X and Y until they have enough energy to react together.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think of ATP as a fuel that is burned. Heat released into the cell is lost, not directed into a specific reaction. Fix: ATP drives work through phosphate transfer that couples it to the reaction, not through heating.

choices.choice_text: The phosphate group acts as a catalyst, so forming XY no longer requires any input of energy.
choices.rationale: Tempting because the phosphate step makes the reaction happen. But a catalyst only lowers activation energy; it cannot make an energy-requiring reaction stop requiring energy. Fix: the energy comes from ATP hydrolysis, which is coupled to the reaction.

choices.choice_text: Forming the XY bond releases energy, and the cell captures that released energy by making ATP from ADP and phosphate.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you reverse the direction of coupling. The stem says forming XY requires energy, and ATP is used up here, not made. Fix: an energy-releasing process (ATP hydrolysis) pays for an energy-requiring one (making XY).

verification: EK 3.3.A.2(ii) energy-releasing processes may be coupled with energy-requiring ones; brief: explain how ATP hydrolysis/phosphate transfer makes an unfavorable process possible. Stem fixes XY formation as energy-requiring and ATP as consumed, which rules out B (heat), C (catalysis), D (reversed).
author_flags: Seed (apoptosis vs necrosis) is off-topic for 3.3 Cellular Energy and was not used; seed_used set false. Phosphorylated-intermediate mechanism is described generically; no specific enzyme or Gibbs equation (CED exclusion respected).

topic_title: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection
stem: Researchers randomly select 400 patient records from a hospital's database covering 2015 to 2024. For each patient, they note whether the patient took a daily vitamin D supplement and whether the patient was later diagnosed with a kidney stone, then compare kidney-stone rates for the two groups. How should this study be classified?

choices.choice_text: An experiment, because the researchers compared a supplement group with a no-supplement group.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you treat any two-group comparison as an experiment — but the researchers never assigned anyone to take or skip the supplement; patients chose for themselves. Fix: an experiment requires the researcher to impose the treatment, not just compare existing groups.

choices.choice_text: A retrospective observational study, because no treatment was imposed and the data come from existing past records.
choices.rationale: No treatment was imposed, so the study is observational. Because the researchers looked back at records of what already happened, rather than following people forward from now, it is retrospective.

choices.choice_text: A prospective observational study, because each patient's diagnosis came after the supplement use.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you judge direction by the order of events in a patient's life — but prospective means the researchers collect data going forward from now. Fix: ask when the researchers gather the data; here they read old records, so it is retrospective.

choices.choice_text: An experiment, because the patient records were selected at random from the database.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you mix up random selection with random assignment — but choosing records at random only helps the sample represent the population; it does not assign a treatment. Fix: look for whether a treatment was assigned, not whether anything was random.

verification: Rests on the brief: experiment = researcher imposes a treatment; observational studies split into prospective (collected going forward) and retrospective (looking back at existing records). Patients self-selected supplement use and the data are past hospital records, so B. Seed (census vs sample) tests a different idea and scenario.

topic_title: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem
stem: Commute times for all workers in a large city are strongly right-skewed, with mean 28 minutes and standard deviation 18 minutes. A researcher takes 1,000 random samples of 50 workers each, computes the mean commute time of each sample, and plots those 1,000 means on one dotplot. Which statement best describes this dotplot?

choices.choice_text: Each dot is one sample's mean; the dotplot is approximately normal, centered near 28 minutes, with standard deviation near 2.5 minutes.
choices.rationale: Each dot is a whole sample's statistic, so this approximates the sampling distribution of the sample mean. By the Central Limit Theorem it is approximately normal for n = 50, centered at the population mean, with spread 18/√50 ≈ 2.5 minutes.

choices.choice_text: Each dot is one worker's commute time; the dotplot is strongly right-skewed, like the population.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you picture the raw data from a sample — but the researcher plotted sample means, not individual workers. Fix: before describing a distribution, name what one dot represents; here it is one sample's mean.

choices.choice_text: Each dot is one worker's commute time; the Central Limit Theorem makes these commute times approximately normal.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think the Central Limit Theorem reshapes the population — but individual commute times stay right-skewed no matter how many samples are taken. Fix: the theorem's normality applies to the distribution of the sample mean, not to individuals.

choices.choice_text: Each dot is one sample's mean; the dotplot is approximately normal, centered near 28 minutes, with standard deviation near 18 minutes.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you assume sample means vary as much as individuals do — but averaging 50 values cancels much of the variation. Fix: the spread of sample means is σ/√n = 18/√50 ≈ 2.5 minutes, much smaller than 18.

verification: python3: 18/math.sqrt(50) = 2.5456 -> 'near 2.5' (key A). Distractor D uses population SD 18 (slip: forgetting division by sqrt(n)). B/C mislabel the dot as an individual; C adds the brief's named trap (CLT makes the population normal). Center = population mean 28.
author_flags: Uses sigma/sqrt(n) for the spread, which the topic's brief mentions only qualitatively ('tightens the spread'); the formula is formalized in later topics (Unit 4 sampling distribution of x-bar). Checker may judge whether quoting ~2.5 is in scope; the item works conceptually even without the number.

stem: A school district selects a simple random sample of 60 parents and finds that 45% favor a later school start time. A full survey of every parent later shows the true proportion is 40%. Which statement about the sample proportion as an estimator of the true proportion is correct?

choices.choice_text: It is biased, because this sample's 45% does not equal the true 40%.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you judge bias from one result — but almost every random sample misses p by some amount just by chance. Fix: bias is about whether the estimator's results center on p across all possible samples, not about one sample's miss.

choices.choice_text: It is biased, but taking a larger random sample would remove the bias.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you treat bias and sampling variability as the same thing — but a larger sample shrinks random scatter, not a systematic lean. Fix: random sampling already makes the estimator unbiased; sample size affects only its spread.

choices.choice_text: It is unbiased, because the sample of 60 parents is large enough for the large-counts condition.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you link unbiasedness to having a big enough sample — but large counts only support a normal approximation. Fix: the estimator is unbiased because its sampling distribution is centered at p, which comes from random sampling, not from sample size.

choices.choice_text: It is unbiased; a 5-point miss in one random sample is chance variation, not a systematic lean.
choices.rationale: Unbiasedness is a long-run property: over every possible random sample, the sample proportion has no systematic over- or underestimate, so its mean equals p. One sample landing 5 points high is consistent with that.

verification: Brief/explainer: unbiased means no systematic over/underestimation; a single sample differing from p does not show bias; bias comes from a method that systematically pulls results one way. SRS -> p-hat unbiased (mu_phat = p). Difference 0.45-0.40 = 0.05 by arithmetic. Seed (thermometer, biased, key D) has a different scenario and the opposite conclusion (seed's answer is 'biased'; this item's is 'unbiased').
author_flags: Key letter D matches the seed's key letter; correct ideas differ (biased vs unbiased).

topic_title: Setting Up a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
stem: A planner suspects that a greater proportion of commuters bike to work in North City than in South City. In a random sample of 200 North City commuters, 46 bike; in an independent random sample of 300 South City commuters, 45 bike. Let p1 = the proportion of all North City commuters who bike and p2 = the proportion of all South City commuters who bike. Which setup is correct for a significance test of the planner's claim?

choices.choice_text: H0: p1 − p2 = 0, Ha: p1 − p2 < 0; pooled proportion = 0.182
choices.rationale: Tempting if you write the alternative without checking which city is p1 — but the claim is that North City (p1) is greater, so p1 − p2 should be positive. Fix: reread the definitions of p1 and p2, then point the inequality the way the claim does.

choices.choice_text: H0: p1 − p2 = 0, Ha: p1 − p2 > 0; pooled proportion = 0.182
choices.rationale: With p1 for North City and p2 for South City, the claim 'North is greater' gives Ha: p1 − p2 > 0. Under H0 there is one common proportion, estimated by pooling: (46 + 45)/(200 + 300) = 91/500 = 0.182.

choices.choice_text: H0: p1 − p2 = 0, Ha: p1 − p2 > 0; pooled proportion = 0.19
choices.rationale: Tempting if you average the two sample proportions, (0.23 + 0.15)/2 — but that ignores the different sample sizes. Fix: pool the counts, (46 + 45)/(200 + 300) = 0.182, so the larger sample gets more weight.

choices.choice_text: H0: p̂1 − p̂2 = 0, Ha: p̂1 − p̂2 > 0; pooled proportion = 0.182
choices.rationale: Tempting because the sample proportions are the numbers you can see — but hypotheses are claims about population parameters, and the sample values are already known (0.23 and 0.15). Fix: write hypotheses with p1 and p2, never p̂1 and p̂2.

verification: python3: phat1 = 46/200 = 0.23, phat2 = 45/300 = 0.15; pooled = 91/500 = 0.182 (key B); unweighted average (0.23+0.15)/2 = 0.19 (distractor C, slip: ignoring sample sizes). A = reversed sign; D = hypotheses about statistics. Pooled formula phat_c = (n1 phat1 + n2 phat2)/(n1+n2) from fact pack 3.12-3.13.

topic_title: Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
stem: A random sample of 120 students at a large school was classified by two variables. Of the 30 students who play an instrument, 10 are in math club and 20 are not. Of the 90 students who do not play an instrument, 14 are in math club and 76 are not. The expected counts for a chi-square test of independence are 6 and 24 (instrument row) and 18 and 72 (no-instrument row). Which statement is correct?

choices.choice_text: The expected-counts condition fails because one expected count, 6, is less than 10, so the test should not be carried out.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you carry over the large-counts threshold of 10 from proportion procedures — but the chi-square condition only requires every expected count to exceed 5. Fix: check expected counts against 5 here; 6 passes.

choices.choice_text: The condition is met, and the instrument/math-club cell contributes (10 − 6)²/10 = 1.6 to the chi-square statistic.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you divide by the observed count because it appears first — but each contribution divides by the expected count. Fix: use (observed − expected)²/expected = (10 − 6)²/6.

choices.choice_text: The condition is met because every expected count exceeds 5, and the instrument/math-club cell contributes (10 − 6)²/6 ≈ 2.67.
choices.rationale: All four expected counts (6, 24, 18, 72) are greater than 5, so the condition holds. That cell's contribution is (observed − expected)²/expected = 16/6 ≈ 2.67.

choices.choice_text: The condition is met, and the instrument/math-club cell contributes (10 − 6)/6 ≈ 0.67 to the chi-square statistic.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you forget to square the difference — but without squaring, positive and negative gaps would cancel across cells. Fix: square first, (10 − 6)² = 16, then divide by 6 to get about 2.67.

verification: python3: expected = row*col/total -> [[6,24],[18,72]] from row totals 30, 90 and column totals 24, 96 (n=120); observed [[10,20],[14,76]] match totals. Contribution (10-6)^2/6 = 2.667 (key C); divide-by-observed slip 16/10 = 1.6 (B); no-square slip 4/6 = 0.667 (D); threshold-10 slip (A). Total chi-square = 4.444 (not used). Expected-count > 5 rule from fact pack 3.14-3.15.
author_flags: Seed asks to compute an expected count; this item gives expected counts and tests the condition threshold and a cell contribution, so the seed's answer is not taught.

stem: A coffee shop owner tests whether more than 30% of customers order oat milk, using H0: p = 0.30 and Ha: p > 0.30. A random sample of customers gives a p-value of 0.04. Which is the correct interpretation of this p-value?

choices.choice_text: If 30% of all customers order oat milk, there is about a 4% chance that a random sample of this size would give a sample proportion as large as or larger than the one observed.
choices.rationale: A p-value is computed assuming H0 is true, and it gives the chance of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, in the direction of Ha. This sentence states both parts in context.

choices.choice_text: There is about a 4% probability that the null hypothesis is true, that is, that exactly 30% of all customers order oat milk.
choices.rationale: Tempting because a small p-value is evidence against H0 — but H0 is a fixed claim, not a random event, so it has no probability here. Fix: the p-value is a probability about sample results, computed assuming H0 is true.

choices.choice_text: Because 1 − 0.04 = 0.96, there is about a 96% probability that more than 30% of all customers order oat milk.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you take 1 − 0.04 as the chance Ha is right — but the p-value says nothing directly about the probability of either hypothesis. Fix: describe how unusual the sample result would be if H0 were true.

choices.choice_text: If more than 30% of all customers order oat milk, there is about a 4% chance of getting a sample proportion as large as or larger than the one observed.
choices.rationale: Tempting because Ha is the owner's claim — but the p-value is calculated under the null model, not the alternative. Fix: always begin the interpretation with 'assuming H0 is true' (here, p = 0.30).

verification: Brief/explainer: p-value = probability, assuming H0 true, of a result at least as extreme as observed; not P(H0 true). Ha: p > 0.30 so 'as large as or larger'. Complement 1 - 0.04 = 0.96 for distractor C. Seed tests the alpha decision rule (alpha 0.01, p 0.047) with a different scenario and correct idea.
author_flags: Choice A is the longest choice, with D of similar length.

stem: The mass spectrum of a natural sample of gallium shows two peaks: one at 68.926 amu with a relative abundance of 60.11% and one at 70.925 amu with a relative abundance of 39.89%. Which choice gives gallium's average atomic mass and correctly explains why the two isotopes differ in mass?

choices.choice_text: 69.93 amu; the heavier isotope has two more neutrons in its nucleus.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you average the two peak masses straight across, as if both isotopes were equally common. But the 68.926 amu isotope is more abundant, so the average must sit closer to it. Fix: multiply each mass by its fractional abundance (0.6011 and 0.3989) before adding.

choices.choice_text: 69.72 amu; the heavier isotope has two more neutrons in its nucleus.
choices.rationale: 68.926 × 0.6011 + 70.925 × 0.3989 = 69.72 amu, a weighted average that lands closer to the more abundant isotope. Isotopes of one element always have the same number of protons, so the 2 amu mass difference comes from two extra neutrons.

choices.choice_text: 69.72 amu; the heavier isotope has two more protons in its nucleus.
choices.rationale: The calculation is right, but the explanation is the classic slip: adding protons would change the element itself, so it would no longer be gallium. Fix: isotopes share a proton count and differ only in neutrons, so the extra mass is from neutrons.

choices.choice_text: 70.13 amu; the heavier isotope has two more neutrons in its nucleus.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you pair each mass with the other peak's abundance, which happens when you read across the spectrum carelessly. That weights the rarer, heavier isotope more, so the answer drifts too high. Fix: match each mass to its own peak height before multiplying.

verification: python3: 68.926*0.6011 + 70.925*0.3989 = 69.7234 -> 69.72 (key). Distractors: simple average (68.926+70.925)/2 = 69.9255 -> 69.93; swapped abundances 68.926*0.3989 + 70.925*0.6011 = 70.1276 -> 70.13; abundances sum to 1.0000. Mass numbers 69 and 71 differ by 2 -> 2 neutrons (brief/explainer: isotope mass difference is from neutrons, not protons or electrons). Single-element, singly charged monatomic ion spectrum, inside the CED exclusion boundary.
author_flags: Gallium isotope masses/abundances are real-world values (Ga-69/Ga-71), used for realism; no figure needed since peaks are given in text.

stem: A liquid hydrocarbon used as a solvent is 89.94% carbon and 10.06% hydrogen by mass. A separate experiment shows its molar mass is 120.2 g/mol. What is the molecular formula of the compound? (Molar masses: C = 12.01 g/mol, H = 1.008 g/mol)

choices.choice_text: C₃H₄
choices.rationale: This is the empirical formula, and stopping here is the most common way to lose the point. C₃H₄ has a mass of only 40.07 g/mol, not 120.2 g/mol. Fix: divide the given molar mass by the empirical formula mass (120.2 ÷ 40.07 = 3) and multiply every subscript by 3.

choices.choice_text: C₉H
choices.rationale: Tempting if you divide the mass percentages by each other (89.94 ÷ 10.06 ≈ 9) without converting to moles first. Mass ratios are not atom ratios because a carbon atom is about 12 times heavier than a hydrogen atom. Fix: convert grams of each element to moles before comparing.

choices.choice_text: C₉H₉
choices.rationale: Tempting if you round the mole ratio 1 : 1.33 down to 1 : 1, giving CH (13.02 g/mol), and then round 120.2 ÷ 13.02 = 9.23 to 9. A ratio of 1.33 is not close enough to round; it signals thirds, and a multiplier like 9.23 that is not a whole number is the warning sign. Fix: multiply 1 : 1.33 by 3 to get the whole-number ratio 3 : 4.

choices.choice_text: C₉H₁₂
choices.rationale: In 100 g there are 89.94 ÷ 12.01 = 7.489 mol C and 10.06 ÷ 1.008 = 9.980 mol H, a 1 : 1.33 ratio that becomes 3 : 4, so the empirical formula is C₃H₄ (40.07 g/mol). Since 120.2 ÷ 40.07 = 3, the molecular formula is C₉H₁₂.

author_flags: Seed was an empirical-formula item (Si/N ceramic); this item uses a different compound, different numbers, and the correct idea is the molecular-formula scaling step, not the empirical formula. Distractor B (C9H) is not a chemically sensible formula; kept because it is the direct result of a named slip.

stem: Sodium (Na, Z = 11) has the ground-state configuration [Ne]3s¹. Potassium (K, Z = 19) is directly below sodium in the periodic table and has a lower first ionization energy. Which choice gives potassium's ground-state electron configuration and an explanation that would earn the reasoning point?

choices.choice_text: [Ar]4s¹; potassium's outermost electron is in a higher shell, farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons, so it feels a weaker Coulombic attraction.
choices.rationale: After argon's 18 electrons, the 19th goes into 4s, which is lower in energy than 3d. That electron is farther from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells, so the attraction (F ∝ q₁q₂/r²) is weaker and less energy is needed to remove it.

choices.choice_text: [Ar]3d¹; potassium's outermost electron is in a d subshell, farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons, so it feels a weaker Coulombic attraction.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you fill subshells in numerical order and put the 19th electron in 3d after 3p. But 4s is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first. Fix: follow the Aufbau order 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d.

choices.choice_text: [Ar]4s¹; potassium is lower in Group 1, and ionization energy decreases going down a group.
choices.rationale: The configuration is right and the statement is true, but naming the trend is not an explanation. A reasoning point needs the cause. Fix: say why the trend happens, using distance from the nucleus and shielding.

choices.choice_text: [Ar]4s¹; potassium has more protons than sodium, and a larger nuclear charge holds the outer electron less tightly.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you link more protons with the lower ionization energy because they both appear in this comparison. But a larger nuclear charge pulls harder, not less. Fix: potassium's extra protons are offset by extra inner shells, so the greater distance and shielding are what weaken the attraction.

verification: Aufbau order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d: K (19 e-) = [Ar]4s1 (brief: fill in order of increasing energy, 4s before 3d). Brief/explainer: IE explanation must use nuclear charge and distance/shielding (Coulomb's law), not a vague 'periodic trend' label. K first IE < Na first IE is standard (CED 1.5/1.7 qualitative reasoning). Not an aufbau exception, no quantum numbers.
author_flags: Seed asked for the Ti2+ ion configuration; this item uses a neutral main-group atom and centres on the Coulomb's-law explanation. Explainer's own example is S vs Al, so a different pair (Na vs K) was used. Choice C is a true statement that fails as reasoning; stem asks for the explanation 'that would earn the reasoning point' to make that unambiguous.

stem: Pauling electronegativities: H = 2.20, S = 2.58, N = 3.04, O = 3.44. A student compares the S–H, N–H, and O–H bonds. Which choice correctly orders the bonds from least polar to most polar and states where the partial negative charge sits in the O–H bond?

choices.choice_text: O–H < N–H < S–H; the partial negative charge is on O.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you mix up 'least' and 'most' or think a bigger electronegativity gap makes a bond more even. A larger difference means a more unequal share, so a more polar bond. Fix: compute each difference (0.38, 0.84, 1.24) and list from smallest to largest.

choices.choice_text: S–H < N–H < O–H; the partial negative charge is on H.
choices.rationale: The order is right, but the charge is backwards. Tempting if you think the less electronegative atom ends up with the electrons. Fix: the more electronegative atom (O, 3.44) pulls the shared electrons toward itself, so O carries the δ−.

choices.choice_text: S–H < N–H < O–H; the partial negative charge is on O.
choices.rationale: The electronegativity differences are 0.38 for S–H, 0.84 for N–H, and 1.24 for O–H, so polarity increases in that order. Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared electrons are pulled toward O, giving O the δ−.

choices.choice_text: All three are bonds between nonmetals, so none of them has any ionic character or partial charges.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you sort bonds into separate 'ionic' and 'covalent' boxes. Bonding is a continuum, and every polar bond already has some ionic character. Fix: use the electronegativity difference, not the metal/nonmetal shortcut, to judge polarity.

verification: python3: dEN S-H = 2.58-2.20 = 0.38; N-H = 3.04-2.20 = 0.84; O-H = 3.44-2.20 = 1.24 -> least to most polar S-H < N-H < O-H; O (3.44) > H (2.20) so delta-negative on O. Reversed order in A; delta- on H in B; 'no ionic character' in D is the brief's named continuum misconception (CED EK 2.1: all polar bonds have some ionic character).
author_flags: Seed asked which bond has the greatest ionic character from a list of metal/nonmetal pairs; this item uses a different bond set (all X–H), asks for a full ranking plus delta-negative placement, and adds the continuum misconception.

stem: A particulate diagram of an aqueous sucrose solution shows 6 sucrose molecules in a box that represents 0.5 L of solution. A second diagram, drawn to the same scale, shows a box that represents 1.5 L of solution. How many sucrose molecules must the second box show for the two diagrams to represent the same concentration?

choices.rationale: Tempting if you assume the same number of particles always means the same concentration. But the second box holds three times the volume, so 6 molecules there would be one-third as concentrated. Fix: compare particles per volume, not raw counts.

Tempting if you scale the count by the volume ratio the wrong way (6 × 0.5 ÷ 1.5). A larger volume needs more particles, not fewer, to keep the same concentration. Fix: since the volume triples, the count must triple.
The first box has 6 ÷ 0.5 L = 12 molecules per liter. To match that in 1.5 L, the box needs 12 × 1.5 = 18 molecules, three times as many in three times the volume.
Tempting if you multiply 6 by 1.5 as though the first box were 1 L. That ignores that the 6 molecules sit in only 0.5 L. Fix: find the particles per liter first (6 ÷ 0.5 = 12), then scale to 1.5 L.

verification: python3: 6/0.5 = 12 per L; 12*1.5 = 18 (key). Distractors: same count 6 (ignores volume, the brief's named point loss); inverted scaling 6*0.5/1.5 = 2; treating first box as 1 L 6*1.5 = 9. Ratio reasoning only; no molality, percent, or colligative calculation (CED 3.8 exclusions respected).
author_flags: Sucrose chosen as a nonelectrolyte so each drawn particle is one molecule. Diagram is described in words; no figure required. Explainer example compares 8 vs 12 particles in a box twice the size; this item uses different numbers and asks for a matching count instead of a comparison.

stem: A beaker contains sand stirred into water in which two different food dyes are completely dissolved. A student wants to isolate the sand and also separate the two dyes from each other. Which plan and reason are both correct?

choices.choice_text: Filter to collect the sand, then pass the colored filtrate through a second, finer filter paper, which traps the dye molecules because they are larger than water molecules.
choices.rationale: Tempting because filtration worked for the sand. But dissolved dye molecules are in the same phase as the water and pass through any ordinary filter paper. Fix: use filtration only for undissolved solids, and use a method based on intermolecular attractions for dissolved parts.

choices.choice_text: Filter to collect the sand, then run chromatography on the filtrate, where the dyes separate because they are attracted differently to the stationary and mobile phases.
choices.rationale: The sand is undissolved, so filtration removes it. The dyes are dissolved, so they need chromatography, which separates them by how strongly each interacts with the stationary phase versus the mobile phase.

choices.choice_text: Run chromatography on the whole mixture, where the sand and each dye travel different distances because larger particles move more slowly up the paper.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you picture chromatography as sorting by size, like a sieve. It actually separates by differences in attraction to the two phases, and sand would just clog the spot. Fix: remove the undissolved sand by filtration first, then reason with interaction strength.

choices.choice_text: Filter to collect the sand, then run chromatography on the filtrate, where the dye most attracted to the stationary phase travels farthest.
choices.rationale: The plan works, but the reasoning is backwards. A dye held strongly by the stationary phase stays near the starting line. Fix: the dye that interacts more strongly with the mobile phase moves farther.

verification: Explainer/CED 3.9: filtration separates only undissolved solids; dissolved solutes pass through, so liquid-solution components cannot be separated by filtration. Chromatography separates by differential interaction strength with stationary vs mobile phases; components interacting more strongly with the mobile phase travel farther. Key B uses both facts; A = named point loss; C = size-based misconception plus unfiltered sand; D = reversed direction.
author_flags: Seed asked why one pigment travels farther (polarity reasoning); this item's correct idea is the filtration-then-chromatography method choice. Distractor D overlaps the seed's concept (direction of travel) but in a different scenario, and its fix restates the general rule, not the seed's answer.

stem: The graph of h is made of two pieces. For x < 2 it is the line y = x + 1, which ends in an open circle at (2, 3). For x ≥ 2 it is the curve y = (x − 2)^2 + 1, which starts with a filled dot at (2, 1). Which statement about lim(x→2) h(x) is true?

choices.choice_text: The limit is 1, because the graph has a filled dot at (2, 1).
choices.rationale: Tempting if you read the filled dot as the limit — but the dot only gives h(2), and the limit is about the y-values the graph approaches from both sides. Fix: trace the curve toward x = 2 from the left and from the right before you look at the dot.

choices.choice_text: It does not exist; the left side approaches 3 but the right side approaches 1.
choices.rationale: From the left the line climbs toward y = 3, and from the right the curve comes down toward y = 1. The two one-sided limits disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist — this is the mismatched one-sided limits pattern.

choices.choice_text: The limit is 3, because the graph approaches y = 3 as x approaches 2.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you only trace the left piece — but the right piece approaches y = 1, not 3. Fix: a two-sided limit needs both sides; check the right-hand behavior too.

choices.choice_text: The limit is 2, the average of the left-side and right-side values.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you try to split the difference between 3 and 1 — but limits are never averaged. Fix: if the one-sided limits differ, the answer is that the two-sided limit does not exist.

verification: sympy: limit(x+1, x, 2, '-') = 3; limit((x-2)**2+1, x, 2, '+') = 1; one-sided limits differ so the two-sided limit DNE (CED canonical mismatched one-sided limits pattern). Distractor values: filled dot h(2)=1 (A), left-only 3 (C), average (3+1)/2 = 2 (D). Explainer fact: 'The filled point shows f(c); nearby curve behavior shows the limit.'
author_flags: Graph is described in words (no figure). Seed answer was 'limit exists = 4 despite isolated point'; this item uses a different idea (mismatched one-sided limits, DNE).

stem:
A function g is defined for all real numbers, and g(1) = 2. A table gives these values near x = 1.

x:    0.9   0.99   0.999   1.001   1.01   1.1
g(x): 4.8   4.98   4.998   5.002   5.02   5.2

Assuming the table shows g's true behavior near x = 1, which statement matches the table and the given value?

choices.choice_text: lim(x→1) g(x) = 5, with an open circle at (1, 5) and a filled dot at (1, 2).
choices.rationale: Both sides of the table close in on 5, so the limit is 5. Since g(1) = 2, the graph shows the approach to 5 as an open circle and the actual value as a separate filled dot at (1, 2). The same limit sentence — as x approaches 1, g(x) approaches 5 — holds in the table, the notation and the graph.

choices.choice_text: lim(x→1) g(x) = 2, because the value of g at x = 1 is g(1) = 2.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you match the limit to the function value — but the table shows outputs closing in on 5, not 2. Fix: the limit comes from the approach trend in the table; g(1) is a separate fact about the point itself.

choices.choice_text: The graph of g has a vertical asymptote at x = 1, because g(1) ≠ 5.
choices.rationale: Tempting if any mismatch at a point feels like a break to infinity — but the outputs stay near 5 and never grow without bound. Fix: a vertical asymptote needs unbounded values near x = 1; here the graph has a hole and a displaced point instead.

choices.choice_text: lim(x→1) g(x) does not exist, because g(1) does not equal 5.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think the limit must equal the function value to exist — but a limit only needs both sides to approach the same number, which they do. Fix: g(1) ≠ 5 makes g discontinuous at 1, but the limit still exists and equals 5.

verification: Table generated from 5 + 2(x − 1) (python3): 4.8, 4.98, 4.998, 5.002, 5.02, 5.2 — both sides approach 5. g(1)=2 given separately, so limit 5 ≠ value 2: removable discontinuity (hole at (1,5), filled point at (1,2)). Explainer fact: same limit sentence across representations; common loss is matching the limit to the function value.
author_flags: No seed. Stem says 'assuming the table shows g's true behavior' so the table-based limit claim is defensible.

stem: A sensor reading must be modeled by a function that is continuous at every x in the closed interval [−1, 3]. Which of the following functions meets that requirement?

choices.rationale: Tempting because rational functions are continuous on their domains — but x^2 − 4 = 0 at x = 2, which lies inside [−1, 3]. Fix: find every excluded x-value, then check whether any of them land inside the interval.

choices.choice_text: f(x) = √x
choices.rationale: Tempting because √x is continuous wherever it is defined — but it is undefined for −1 ≤ x < 0, the left part of this interval. Fix: check the domain against the whole interval, endpoints included.
The denominator factors as (x − 4)(x + 2), so the only excluded values are x = 4 and x = −2. Neither is in [−1, 3], so this rational function is continuous at every point of the interval.

choices.choice_text: f(x) = x^2 for x < 1, and f(x) = 2x for x ≥ 1
choices.rationale: Tempting because both pieces are polynomials — but at the boundary x = 1 the left piece approaches 1 while the right piece gives 2, a jump. Fix: at every piecewise boundary inside the interval, check that the left limit, right limit and function value all match.

verification: sympy continuous_domain over the reals: (x+1)/(x^2-4) excludes ±2 (2 ∈ [−1,3]); sqrt(x) is [0, ∞) (misses [−1,0)); 1/(x^2−2x−8) = 1/((x−4)(x+2)) excludes 4 and −2, interval [−1,3] is a subset of its continuous domain (True); piecewise: limit x^2 at 1− = 1, 2x at 1+ = 2, jump.
author_flags: Seed used tan/ln families on [0,4]; this item uses rational/root/piecewise on [−1,3] with a different correct function.

topic_title: Connecting Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes
stem: Let f(x) = 2x/(x − 3). Which statement correctly describes the behavior of f near x = 3?

choices.choice_text: lim(x→3⁻) f(x) = ∞ and lim(x→3⁺) f(x) = ∞, so x = 3 is a vertical asymptote.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you see a zero denominator and assume both sides blow up the same way — but for x just below 3 the denominator is a small negative number while the numerator is near 6, so f is very negative. Fix: check the sign of the numerator and denominator on each side separately.

choices.choice_text: lim(x→3⁻) f(x) = −∞ and lim(x→3⁺) f(x) = ∞, so x = 3 is a vertical asymptote.
choices.rationale: Near x = 3 the numerator is about 6. From the left the denominator is a tiny negative number, so f drops without bound; from the right it is a tiny positive number, so f grows without bound. Either infinite one-sided limit makes x = 3 a vertical asymptote.

choices.choice_text: lim(x→3) f(x) does not exist, so f has no vertical asymptote at x = 3.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you stop at 'does not exist' — but the reason it fails to exist is unbounded growth, which is exactly what a vertical asymptote is. Fix: describe each side with an infinite limit and then name x = 3 as the asymptote.

choices.choice_text: lim(x→3) f(x) = 2, because the ratio of leading coefficients is 2.
choices.rationale: Tempting if you mix up end behavior with behavior near a finite input — the leading-coefficient ratio gives the limit as x → ∞, which is the horizontal asymptote y = 2. Fix: for x → 3, plug in values close to 3 and check signs; for x → ∞, compare leading terms.

verification: sympy: limit(2x/(x−3), x, 3, '-') = −oo; limit(..., x, 3, '+') = +oo; limit(..., x, oo) = 2 (source of distractor D). Brief: write the infinite limit and name x = c as the vertical asymptote; common loss: writing only DNE (distractor C).
author_flags: Seed asked to find all vertical asymptotes of a rational function with a hole; this item asks for one-sided infinite-limit description, different function and idea.

topic_title: Connecting Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes
stem: Let f(x) = (3x^2 − 5x)/(6x^2 + x − 2). Which of the following gives the horizontal asymptote of the graph of f?

choices.rationale: Tempting if you take the ratio of leading coefficients upside down (6/3) — but the limit at infinity is numerator's leading coefficient over the denominator's. Fix: for equal degrees, divide every term by x^2 and let x → ∞; you get 3/6.

Tempting because 6x^2 + x − 2 = (2x − 1)(3x + 2) is zero at x = 1/2 — but that gives a vertical asymptote, not a horizontal one. Fix: a horizontal asymptote is a y = L line from end behavior; an x = c line comes from a finite input where f is unbounded.
Tempting if you evaluate f near x = 0, where f(0) = 0 — but end behavior is about x → ∞ and x → −∞, not x → 0. Fix: write lim(x→∞) f(x) and lim(x→−∞) f(x), then compare leading terms.
The numerator and denominator have the same degree, so as x → ±∞ the leading terms dominate: 3x^2/(6x^2) = 1/2. Since lim(x→∞) f(x) = lim(x→−∞) f(x) = 1/2, the only horizontal asymptote is y = 1/2.

verification: sympy: limit(f, x, oo) = 1/2, limit(f, x, −oo) = 1/2; factor(6x^2+x−2) = (2x−1)(3x+2) → vertical asymptote x = 1/2 (distractor B, no common factor with x(3x−5)); f(0) = 0 (distractor C, fact-pack documented 'evaluating near zero' misconception); 6/3 = 2 (distractor A, inverted ratio).
author_flags: Seed was a square-root function with two different horizontal asymptotes; this is a rational function with one, built around the x = 1/2 vs y = 1/2 confusion.

topic_title: Estimating Derivatives of a Function at a Point
stem:
The temperature of a cup of coffee, T(t), in degrees Celsius, is measured t minutes after it is poured. T is differentiable.

t (minutes):  0    2    5    6    9
T(t) (°C):   70   64   57   55   48

Using the nearest listed times on each side of t = 5, estimate T′(5).

choices.choice_text: −22/9 °C per minute
choices.rationale: Tempting if you use the first and last rows, (48 − 70)/(9 − 0) — but that is an average rate over the whole 9 minutes, not a local estimate at t = 5. Fix: use the closest times that bracket t = 5, which are t = 2 and t = 6.

choices.choice_text: −4/9 °C per minute
choices.rationale: Tempting if you divide the change in time by the change in temperature, (6 − 2)/(55 − 64) — but that flips the slope (and its units would be minutes per degree). Fix: a derivative estimate is change in output over change in input, ΔT/Δt.

choices.choice_text: −9/4 °C per minute
choices.rationale: The nearest times on each side of 5 are t = 2 and t = 6, so T′(5) ≈ (55 − 64)/(6 − 2) = −9/4. The coffee is cooling at about 2.25 °C per minute at t = 5; this is a secant-slope estimate, not the exact derivative.

choices.choice_text: 9/4 °C per minute
choices.rationale: Tempting if you subtract temperatures in one order and times in the other, (64 − 55)/(6 − 2) — but that flips the sign, and the coffee is cooling. Fix: keep the same order on top and bottom: (T(6) − T(2))/(6 − 2).

verification: python3 Fraction: key (55−64)/(6−2) = −9/4; distant endpoints (48−70)/(9−0) = −22/9; inverted (6−2)/(55−64) = −4/9; mixed-order sign slip (64−55)/(6−2) = 9/4. Checked no collision with other plausible estimates (backward (57−64)/3 = −7/3, forward (55−57)/1 = −2; neither is a choice).
author_flags: Seed also uses a nearest-bracketing difference quotient but with the target not in the table; this item puts the target in the table (symmetric bracketing around a listed point) in a units context. Stem specifies the method so forward/backward one-sided estimates are not competing answers. Choice B is labeled °C per minute for parallel form though its true units would be minutes per °C — rationale says so; checker may prefer a different label.
